Suicide is unbelievably difficult for the people that are left behind. One thing I'd urge you to understand is that survivor's guilt is a very fucking real thing. It's the burden of those left behind, whose naturally human tendency is to retro-project a problem that they should have seen, and this forms the scaffold for the creation of a totally fictional narrative of things you should have noticed and points where you could have intervened on the timeline to change the person's path.

You've got to just let yourself drop those ideas. They are your creation. You simply cannot retro-project responsibility onto past events that you weren't interpreting in light of information that only came later.

The responsibility to go on being, to keep holding up the project of Being, is every single individuals (and no one else's); likewise, it is every single individual's choice to end the project. It is hard because of the way you perceive your proximity to the person, and the causal chain. You are presuming things that you can't, however: that since your last encounter with him was only hours prior to the event, that something should have tipped you off because suicidal "signals" must amplify the closer a person gets to the moment.

That isn't true. At all. I once worked with a woman who I would have told you was completely adjusted. One day, on the her wedding anniversary, she was sitting with her husband and two children in their living room. She calmly stood up, walked into the adjacent bedroom and shot herself in the head, with just a wall between herself and her family.

We cannot pretend to know what that woman's experience was like. What was going on in there. How she was interpreting her world, and how it was impacting her expectations for the future. We can only say that her expectations for the future were bleak, insofar as she didn't find it worth it to be around for them. While this can cause us terrible sadness, wishing that we'd only known what her experience/interpretation of the world was so that maybe we could have impacted it, we have to be careful not to transfer her responsibility onto ourselves. It is the same with your friend.

The anger that you feel toward him is quite natural. Anger comes from an indignation that some aspect of your personal sphere (your own sphere of being) has been attacked by another person without due cause. When we feel there is due cause, we experience it as either anxiety or depression. Anger is something specific: something or someone has taken something from me that I didn't deserve to have taken.

And you're right. You didn't. Neither did your other friends or his family.

The only advice I can offer with regard to the really fucking difficult emotions you are going to feel is to try to augment your beliefs about his situation so that they impact your personal landscape differently. Try to meditate on the fact - really internalize it - that he didn't do this to intentionally cut something out of the lives or experience of his loved ones. He loved you all. Something in his experience of the world and the way he was interpreting it caused his personal sphere to shrink, always in an interpretative state of loss or potential loss, this impacted his expectations for the future as being one in which he couldn't grow, nothing would change, and only further loss would remain. It's a runaway spiral.

He did this because he undervalued his own power/place in the world and saw it as under an ongoing attack that was never going to get better. This is not your fault. You don't have privileged access to these maps of the world that exist in other minds. It's not your fault that he didn't reach out and try to tell you about it - the fucking worst part about these problems is that there isn't some reasonable interlocutor inside of him that can show him his interpretative framework is a problem - your friend just took his interpretation as reality. Hence, there was no reason for him to reach out to you for correction, just help - and so many people are afraid to ask for help. For the massively depressed, they often don't see help as a solution. They don't believe anyone can help, there is something fundamental about themselves or the world that talk and sharing cannot change.

Emotions are the results of automatic thoughts and how you pre-rationally interpret those automatic thoughts. They are a very difficult thing to change, impossible really to just eliminate. Every time you feel something painful as the result of this, try to be very quiet and identify exactly what you thought right before the emotion washed over you. You might discover some automatic thoughts you are having, showcasing certain beliefs that are not calibrated to reality. I've mentioned the beliefs above that are sourced from guilt: "I should have been there, or reached out." No, you couldn't have done anything more than you did, not unless reality itself had changed. You have to let the past go.

There is a book I like called 'How to Be a Stoic' by Massimo Pigliucci. It has a segment on grief from suicide in it. This is not a book to get a very deep dive into stoicism, which is a philosophy that is a lot deeper than the cursory descriptions you get of it in modern culture. But, for a start it is a good launch pad into stoicism, and you may find the grief segment very helpful. Stoicism is not a complete answer in my opinion, but more than any other thread of thought out there, it takes head on the nature of our relationship to emotion and actually describes the situation realistically.
